title: Benford's Law: Why Do Numbers Prefer to Start with One?
question: Why do the leading digits of real-world data, from river lengths to tax returns, favor 1 over 9 by a factor of six?
summary: In many natural datasets about 30% of numbers begin with 1 and under 5% with 9. The pattern comes from scale invariance, and it is now used to catch fraud.
content:
A Worn Page in the Logarithm Table

In 1881 the astronomer Simon Newcomb noticed that the early pages of library logarithm tables were dirtier than the later ones. People looked up numbers beginning with 1 far more often than numbers beginning with 9. Frank Benford rediscovered the effect in 1938 and tested it on river lengths, street addresses, atomic weights and population figures. The leading digit d appears with probability log10(1 + 1/d): about 30.1% for 1, 17.6% for 2, and only 4.6% for 9.

The Core Intuition: Growth Spends Longer Starting With One

Think of a quantity growing 10% a year, such as a bank balance of 1,000. To climb from 1,000 to 2,000 it must double, which takes about seven years. From 9,000 to 10,000 it needs only about a 11% rise, roughly one year. The balance sits in the 1xxx range for the same amount of time it takes to double, but in the 9xxx range for only one step. Whenever a process is multiplicative, the number spends a fixed fraction of its journey in each leading digit, and that fraction is proportional to the logarithmic width of the interval.

Scale Invariance Forces the Answer

A sharper argument says that if there is any universal law for leading digits, it must not care about units. Convert a dataset from dollars to euros, or from miles to kilometers, and the leading-digit distribution should not change. Ted Hill proved in 1995 that the logarithmic distribution is the only one that survives all such rescalings. Data that spans several orders of magnitude and arises from mixing many distributions tends toward Benford, in the same way that sums converge toward the bell curve.

When It Fails, and Why That Is Useful

Benford's law does not hold for heights of adults, lottery numbers or phone numbers. These have a narrow range, a built-in cap, or assigned values. That failure is the key to its practical use. Forensic accountants compare the leading digits of reported figures against the expected curve, since people inventing numbers tend to spread digits evenly, and they overuse 5s and 6s. Analyses of Enron-era accounts, of Greek economic statistics before euro entry, and of election returns have all used the test as a screening tool. It flags suspicion rather than proving guilt, because honest data can deviate for legitimate reasons.

What It Says About Numbers

The law reveals that our decimal digits are not neutral labels. The way we write numbers interacts with how quantities grow in the world, so the first digit encodes something about the logarithm of the magnitude. A mild mystery remains: why so many natural datasets are broad and multiplicative enough to qualify.

perspectives.title: Mathematical
perspectives.description: Benford's distribution is the unique scale-invariant, and base-invariant, law for significant digits. It is a statement about the uniform distribution of the logarithm modulo 1.

perspectives.title: Forensic accounting
perspectives.description: Human fabricators have poor intuitions about randomness. Deviations from Benford in invoices or expense claims give auditors a cheap first filter before costly manual checks.

perspectives.title: Physical
perspectives.description: Processes governed by exponential growth or decay, such as populations, radioactive decay and compound interest, naturally generate logarithmically uniform values.

perspectives.title: Epistemological
perspectives.description: A pattern that holds regardless of units suggests it reflects structure in how we measure, not in any particular physical quantity.

openQuestions: Why do so many empirical datasets satisfy the mixing conditions that produce Benford behavior?
Can sophisticated fraudsters simply generate Benford-conforming fake data, and what then catches them?
Does the second or third digit distribution give a more robust test than the first?
Is there a deeper link between Benford's law and Zipf's law?
